village.title: Val'Quirico
paragraphs: Val'Quirico is a walled, pedestrian village built in the style of a medieval Tuscan town on the grounds of an old hacienda, Santa Águeda, in the state of Tlaxcala. Think stone houses, wooden balconies, lanterns and narrow streets lined with restaurants, cafés and small shops.
It is compact and easy to walk. From any lodging inside the village you can reach the hacienda on foot.

items.title: An open-air courtyard, under a tent
items.text: We are outdoors but covered. The tent keeps off sun and any surprise shower, and evenings get cool, so bring a layer.

items.title: Cobblestones everywhere
items.text: The streets are uneven stone. Thin heels and cobblestones do not get along. See the dress and weather page for shoe advice.

items.title: High altitude
items.text: The village sits at roughly 2,200 metres (about 7,200 feet). Drink water, go easy on the first drink, and use sunscreen during the day.

items.title: Everything on foot

travel.title: Getting there
travel.lead: Most guests will fly into Mexico City or Puebla, then travel by road. Here is how the pieces fit.

items.name: Puebla International Airport (Hermanos Serdán)
items.text: By far the closest: roughly {{dist:20}} from Val'Quirico. It is a small airport with limited routes, including some flights from the US. Worth checking first.

items.name: Mexico City International Airport (Benito Juárez, AICM)
items.text: The widest choice of flights from the US and Brazil. About {{dist:115}} by road. Traffic leaving Mexico City can add a lot of time, especially on Friday afternoons.

items.name: Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA)
items.text: Mexico City's newer airport, north of the city, served by some airlines. [TODO: confirm drive time to Val'Quirico; our estimate is based on the drive to Puebla.]

items.title: Wedding shuttle

items.title: Private driver
items.text: The most comfortable option from Mexico City, door to door. [TODO: recommended driver or transfer company, with prices and WhatsApp]

items.title: Bus to Puebla, then taxi
items.text: Estrella Roja runs direct coaches from Mexico City airport (both terminals) to Puebla. Allow 2 to 2½ hours, more in traffic. From Puebla, Val'Quirico is {{dist:22}} away, around 30 minutes by taxi or app ride.

items.title: Uber and DiDi
items.text: Both work in Puebla and from Puebla airport. Getting a car out of Val'Quirico late at night can take a while, so book return rides ahead when you can.

items.title: Rental car
items.text: Handy if you plan to explore. Take the Mexico City–Puebla toll road (150D), exit at Xoxtla, and you are a couple of kilometres away. Keep cash or a card for tolls, and avoid long drives after dark.

entry.title: Passports and entry
entry.disclaimer: Entry rules change. This is a friendly summary from November 2026, not legal advice. Always confirm with the Mexican consulate or the National Migration Institute (INM), and with your airline, before you book.

groups.title: US citizens
groups.text: A valid passport book is required to fly. No visa is needed for tourist visits of up to 180 days; the officer decides the length of stay on arrival.

groups.title: Brazilian citizens
groups.text: Brazilians need a visa to visit Mexico. Since February 2026 an electronic visa (e-Visa) is again available for those arriving by air; apply online before you fly. You may be exempt if you hold a valid visa or permanent residence for the United States, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom or the Schengen area. Check the current rules early, as they have changed more than once.

groups.title: Mexican citizens
groups.text: Nothing special. Bring an official ID for hotels.

groups.title: Everyone else
groups.text: Requirements depend on your passport and on any visas you already hold. Check the INM or your nearest Mexican consulate.

entry.tips: Whatever your passport, make sure it stays valid for your whole trip, keep the entry record or passport stamp you receive on arrival, and consider travel insurance.

explore.title: Things to do
explore.lead: You are flying a long way, so make a trip of it. Everything here is a day trip or less from Val'Quirico.
explore.note: Drive times are approximate and depend on traffic.

places.name: Val'Quirico
places.text: Wander the lanes, pick a terrace, order something with mezcal. The village is at its best early in the morning and after dark, when the lanterns come on.

places.name: Cacaxtla & Xochitécatl
places.text: A hilltop archaeological site close to the village, known for some of the best-preserved pre-Hispanic murals in Mexico.

places.name: Puebla
places.text: A UNESCO World Heritage centre with a vast cathedral, the gilded Rosary Chapel, Talavera pottery workshops and the home of mole poblano. Eat a cemita while you are there.

places.name: Cholula
places.text: Climb the Great Pyramid, the largest by volume in the world, to the yellow church on top. On a clear morning the Popocatépetl volcano fills the horizon.

places.name: Tlaxcala
places.text: The small, calm state capital: an orange-and-red main square, murals that tell the history of the Tlaxcaltecas, and one of the oldest churches in the Americas.

places.name: Atlixco
places.text: A flower-growing town at the foot of the volcano, with nurseries, rooftop terraces and good ice cream.

places.name: Mexico City
places.text: If you are landing there anyway, give it a few days: museums, markets, and some of the best restaurants on the continent.

muertos.title: Arriving early?
muertos.text: Day of the Dead is celebrated on November 1 and 2, the weekend before the wedding. Puebla, Tlaxcala and Atlixco fill with marigolds, altars and parades. It is a beautiful reason to come a few days ahead.

attire.title: Dress & weather
attire.lead: Early November is dry season in central Mexico: bright warm days, and evenings that cool down fast once the sun sets around 6 pm.

weather.title: The weather
weather.text: At this altitude the sun is strong and the shade is cool. Rain is unlikely in November. After dark you will want a jacket, a shawl or a wrap, even under the tent.
weather.source: Based on climate averages for nearby Puebla. Check the forecast the week before.

shoes.title: Shoes
shoes.text: The village is paved in cobblestones. Block heels, wedges or elegant flats will carry you through the night. Stilettos will get stuck between the stones. If you can't live without them, bring a second pair for walking.

pack.title: Worth packing
items: A warm layer for the evening
Comfortable shoes for the Friday and Sunday events
A power adapter if you are coming from Brazil. Mexico uses the same flat-pin plugs as the US, at 127 V.

items.q: What currency should I bring? Cash or card?
items.a: Mexico uses the peso (MXN). Cards are accepted at most hotels and restaurants, including in Val'Quirico. Carry some cash, say {{mxn:1000}} to {{mxn:2000}} in small notes, for tips, taxis, tolls and market stalls. Bank ATMs give the best rates; if the machine offers to convert to your home currency, decline.

In restaurants, 10 to 15% is customary and is usually not included in the bill. When you pay by card, tell the server the percentage before they charge you. A few pesos are appreciated by porters, valets and people who help with bags.

items.q: Will my phone work? What about Wi-Fi?
items.a: Many US plans include Mexico at no extra cost; check with your carrier. Otherwise a travel eSIM or a local prepaid SIM (Telcel has the best coverage) is cheap and easy. Hotels and most restaurants have Wi-Fi. Everyone in Mexico uses WhatsApp, so install it before you travel.

Val'Quirico is a private, walkable development that feels relaxed, and Puebla and Tlaxcala are well-visited by travellers. Use the same common sense as on any trip: take registered taxis or app rides, avoid driving long distances at night, and keep valuables out of sight. Please also read your own government's current travel advice for Mexico.

items.q: Can I drink the tap water?
items.a: Stick to bottled or filtered water, which is what restaurants and hotels serve.

The streets of the village are cobbled and uneven, which can be hard going with a wheelchair, walker or stroller. [TODO: confirm step-free access, drop-off point and accessible restrooms at the hacienda.] Tell us what you need in the RSVP and we will arrange it.
November is the dry season, so rain is unlikely. If it does rain, the whole celebration is under a large tent.
Central Mexico is on UTC−6 all year, with no daylight saving time. That is three hours behind Brasília.

items.q: When should I arrive and leave?
items.a: To enjoy everything, arrive by Friday afternoon, {{date:2027-11-05}}, and leave on Sunday afternoon or later. If you fly out of Mexico City on Sunday, book an evening flight.
